subject: chemistry
question_text: Why are solids rigid?
answer_text: The intermolecular forces of attraction that are present in solids are very strong. The constituent particles of solids cannot move from their positions i.e., they have fixed positions. However, they can oscillate about their mean positions. This is the reason solids are rigid.
final_answer: Thus, solids are rigid due to strong intermolecular forces and fixed positions of particles.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of intermolecular forces and particle behavior.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Why do solids have a definite volume?
answer_text: The intermolecular forces of attraction that are present in solids are very strong. The constituent particles of solids have fixed positions i.e., they are rigid. Hence, solids have a definite volume.
final_answer: Therefore, solids possess a definite volume due to strong intermolecular forces and fixed positions of particles.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of solid structure and intermolecular forces.

difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding the properties of glass and liquids.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Refractive index of a solid is observed to have the same value along all directions. Comment on the nature of this solid. Would it show cleavage property?
answer_text: An isotropic solid has the same value of physical properties when measured along different directions. Therefore, the given solid, having the same value of refractive index along all directions, is isotropic in nature. Hence, the solid is an amorphous solid. When an amorphous solid is cut with a sharp edged tool, it cuts into two pieces with irregular surfaces.
final_answer: Thus, the solid is isotropic and does not show cleavage property.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of isotropic properties and cleavage.

question_text: Classify the following solids in different categories based on the nature of intermolecular forces operating in them: Potassium sulphate, tin, benzene, urea, ammonia, water, zinc sulphide, graphite, rubidium, argon, silicon carbide.
answer_text: Potassium sulphate → Ionic solid; Tin → Metallic solid; Benzene → Molecular (non-polar) solid; Urea → Polar molecular solid; Ammonia → Polar molecular solid; Water → Hydrogen bonded molecular solid; Zinc sulphide → Ionic solid; Graphite → Covalent or network solid; Rubidium → Metallic solid; Argon → Non-polar molecular solid; Silicon carbide → Covalent or network solid.
final_answer: Thus, the classification is based on the nature of intermolecular forces.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Ionic solids conduct electricity in molten state but not in solid state. Explain.
answer_text: In ionic compounds, electricity is conducted by ions. In solid state, ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces and are not free to move about within the solid. Hence, ionic solids do not conduct electricity in solid state. However, in molten state or in solution form, the ions are free to move and can conduct electricity.
final_answer: Therefore, ionic solids conduct electricity only in molten state due to free movement of ions.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding ionic conductivity and states of matter.

difficulty_reasoning: Direct recall of properties of metallic solids.

question_text: Give the significance of a 'lattice point'.

question_text: Explain how much portion of an atom located at (i) corner and (ii) body-centre of a cubic unit cell is part of its neighbouring unit cell.

parts.part_text: An atom located at the corner of a cubic unit cell is shared by eight adjacent unit cells.
parts.answer_text: Therefore, the portion of the atom is shared by one unit cell.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the contribution of the corner atom to one unit cell is 1/8.

parts.part_text: An atom located at the body centre of a cubic unit cell is not shared by its neighbouring unit cell.
parts.answer_text: Therefore, the atom belongs only to the unit cell in which it is present i.e., its contribution to the unit cell is 1.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the contribution of the body-centre atom to one unit cell is 1.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of atomic positioning in unit cells.

question_text: What type of defect can arise when a solid is heated? Which physical property is affected by it and in what way?
answer_text: When a solid is heated, vacancy defect can arise. A solid crystal is said to have vacancy defect when some of the lattice sites are vacant. Vacancy defect leads to a decrease in the density of the solid.
final_answer: Thus, vacancy defect leads to a decrease in the density of the solid.

answer_text: (i) ZnS shows Frenkel defect. (ii) AgBr shows Frenkel defect as well as Schottky defect.

question_text: Explain how vacancies are introduced in an ionic solid when a cation of higher valence is added as an impurity in it.
answer_text: When a cation of higher valence is added to an ionic solid as an impurity, it replaces more than one cation of lower valence to keep the crystal electrically neutral. As a result, some sites become vacant.
final_answer: Thus, vacancies are introduced in the ionic solid.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of ionic solids and the effects of impurities.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Ionic solids, which have anionic vacancies due to metal excess defect, develop colour. Explain with the help of a suitable example.
answer_text: The colour develops because of the presence of electrons in the anionic sites. These electrons absorb energy from the visible part of radiation and get excited. For example, when crystals of NaCl are heated in an atmosphere of sodium vapours, the sodium atoms get deposited on the surface of the crystal and the chloride ions from the crystal diffuse to the surface to form NaCl with the deposited Na atoms.
final_answer: Thus, the presence of electrons in anionic sites leads to colour development in ionic solids.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of defects and their optical properties.

question_text: Explain (i) The basis of similarities and differences between metallic and ionic crystals. (ii) Ionic solids are hard and brittle.

parts.part_text: The basis of similarities and differences between metallic and ionic crystals.
parts.answer_text: The basis of similarities between metallic and ionic crystals is that both these crystal types are held by the electrostatic force of attraction. In metallic crystals, the electrostatic force acts between the positive ions and the electrons. In ionic crystals, it acts between the oppositely-charged ions. Hence, both have high melting points.
parts.final_answer: Thus, both types of crystals exhibit high melting points due to strong electrostatic forces.

parts.part_text: Ionic solids are hard and brittle.
parts.answer_text: The constituent particles of ionic crystals are ions. These ions are held together in three-dimensional arrangements by the electrostatic force of attraction. Since the electrostatic force of attraction is very strong, the charged ions are held in fixed positions. This is the reason why ionic crystals are hard and brittle.
parts.final_answer: Therefore, ionic solids are hard and brittle due to strong ionic bonds.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of crystal structures and properties.

subject: chemistry
question_text: What is a semiconductor? Describe the two main types of semiconductors and contrast their conduction mechanism.
answer_text: Semiconductors are substances having conductance in the intermediate range of 10^-6 to 10^4 ohm^-1 m^-1. The two main types of semiconductors are n-type and p-type. n-type semiconductors have increased conductivity due to negatively-charged electrons, while p-type semiconductors have increased conductivity due to electron holes.
final_answer: Thus, n-type semiconductors conduct through electrons, while p-type semiconductors conduct through holes.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of semiconductor types and their mechanisms.

question_text: Non-stoichiometric cuprous oxide, CuO can be prepared in laboratory. In this oxide, copper to oxygen ratio is slightly less than 2:1. Can you account for the fact that this substance is a p-type semiconductor?

question_image.description: Image related to cuprous oxide and its semiconductor properties.

answer_text: In the cuprous oxide (CuO) prepared in the laboratory, copper to oxygen ratio is slightly less than 2:1. This means that the number of Cu+ ions is slightly less than twice the number of O2- ions. This is because some Cu+ ions have been replaced by Cu2+ ions. Every Cu2+ ion replaces two Cu+ ions, thereby creating holes. As a result, the substance conducts electricity with the help of these positive holes. Hence, the substance is a p-type semiconductor.

steps.description: Identify the copper to oxygen ratio in cuprous oxide.
Explain the replacement of Cu+ ions by Cu2+ ions.
Conclude that the presence of holes allows for electrical conductivity.

final_answer: Therefore, the substance is a p-type semiconductor.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of semiconductor properties and ion replacement.

question_text: Explain the following with suitable examples: (i) Ferromagnetism (ii) Paramagnetism (iii) Ferrimagnetism (iv) Antiferromagnetism (v) 12-16 and 13-15 group compounds.

parts.part_text: Ferromagnetism: The substances that are strongly attracted by a magnetic field are called ferromagnetic substances. Ferromagnetic substances can be permanently magnetised even in the absence of a magnetic field. Some examples of ferromagnetic substances are iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and CrO. In solid state, the metal ions of ferromagnetic substances are grouped together into small regions called domains and each domain acts as a tiny magnet. In an un-magnetised piece of a ferromagnetic substance, the domains are randomly-oriented and so, their magnetic moments get cancelled. However, when the substance is placed in a magnetic field, all the domains get oriented in the direction of the magnetic field. As a result, a strong magnetic effect is produced. This ordering of domains persists even after the removal of the magnetic field. Thus, the ferromagnetic substance becomes a permanent magnet.

Paramagnetism: The substances that are attracted by a magnetic field are called paramagnetic substances. Some examples of paramagnetic substances are O, Cu2t, Fe3t, and Cr3t. Paramagnetic substances get magnetised in a magnetic field in the same direction, but lose magnetism when the magnetic field is removed. To undergo paramagnetism, a substance must have one or more unpaired electrons. This is because the unpaired electrons are attracted by a magnetic field, thereby causing paramagnetism.

subject: chemistry
question_text: What is ferrimagnetism and how does it differ from ferromagnetism?
answer_text: Ferrimagnetism refers to substances where the magnetic moments of domains are aligned in parallel and anti-parallel directions, but in unequal numbers. This results in a weak attraction to magnetic fields compared to ferromagnetic substances.
final_answer: Thus, ferrimagnetic substances exhibit a unique magnetic behavior distinct from ferromagnetic materials.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of magnetic properties and their differences.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain antiferromagnetism and its characteristics.
answer_text: Antiferromagnetism is characterized by domain structures similar to ferromagnetic substances, but with oppositely-oriented domains that cancel each other's magnetic moments.
final_answer: Therefore, antiferromagnetic materials exhibit no net magnetization due to this cancellation.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding the concept of magnetic domains and their orientations.

subject: chemistry
question_text: What are the 12-16 and 13-15 group compounds, and how are they prepared?
answer_text: The 12-16 group compounds are formed by combining group 12 and group 16 elements, while the 13-15 group compounds are formed by combining group 13 and group 15 elements. These compounds are prepared to achieve an average valence of four, similar to Ge or Si.
final_answer: Examples include zinc sulphide (ZnS) and gallium arsenide (GaAs), which are significant in semiconductor technology.
